Buckminster Fuller was an American visionary inventor, architect, and systems theorist who lived from 1895 to 1983. He pioneered the geodesic dome and championed holistic design principles that treated buildings as efficient solutions to human problems. Convinced that technology and rational design could solve humanity's challenges, Fuller became an icon of nineteen-sixties futurism and technological optimism, designing structures that minimized material use while maximizing strength and living space.

Initially, Fuller failed at multiple ventures before finding success in architecture and invention. His persistence and unconventional thinking defined his career arc. He invented the geodesic dome, a structure of interconnected triangular facets that distributes stress evenly, enabling large enclosed spaces with minimal material. It was stronger, lighter, and cheaper than conventional architecture. He designed the iconic Unisphere for the 1964 New York World's Fair, a massive geodesic sphere symbolizing global interconnection and technological mastery during the Cold War space race.

Fuller created the Montreal Expo 67 dome, which housed the U.S. pavilion and became an instant landmark, capturing the era's space-age aesthetic and optimism. He developed the concept of "Spaceship Earth," a systemic view of the planet as a closed system requiring rational resource management and global cooperation—an early articulation of ecological thinking. Fuller promoted "doing more with less," advocating for design efficiency and sustainability principles decades before environmentalism became mainstream. He was a prolific writer and speaker who offered philosophical and often utopian visions of technology serving humanity, and his intellectual reach extended far beyond architecture into systems theory and social thought. Fuller remained active until his death in 1983, adapting his ideas to emerging concerns and maintaining influence on architects, designers, and futurist thinkers.
